What is the primary purpose of insurance?
A) To earn high returns on money invested  
B) To protect against financial loss from unexpected events  
C) To increase the value of savings over time  
D) To replace the need for budgeting

What is the primary purpose of insurance?
A) To earn high returns on money invested  
B) To protect against financial loss from unexpected events  
C) To increase the value of savings over time  
D) To replace the need for budgeting
questions.a:
B) To protect against financial loss from unexpected events  
A student who chooses A or C confuses insurance with investment, not understanding that insurance is about risk transfer, not wealth growth. This reveals a fundamental mix-up between the protective role of insurance and the growth-oriented role of investment.

questions.q:
Why is paying a health insurance premium not considered an investment, even though money is paid regularly?
A) Because the money is refunded at the end of the year  
B) Because it does not generate income or appreciate in value; it only provides coverage for medical expenses  
C) Because only rich people can afford it  
D) Because it is not offered by banks

Why is paying a health insurance premium not considered an investment, even though money is paid regularly?
A) Because the money is refunded at the end of the year  
B) Because it does not generate income or appreciate in value; it only provides coverage for medical expenses  
C) Because only rich people can afford it  
D) Because it is not offered by banks
questions.a:
B) Because it does not generate income or appreciate in value; it only provides coverage for medical expenses  
If a student thinks health insurance is an investment (choosing A or C), they misunderstand that investments must have potential for return—like interest or capital gain. Insurance premiums are a cost for protection, not a vehicle for growth, revealing a confusion between expense and asset-building.

questions.q:
Rohan pays ₹2,000 per year for a mobile insurance plan that covers accidental damage. If his phone screen repair costs ₹8,000 and he makes one claim in a year, what is his net financial benefit from having insurance?
A) ₹6,000  
B) ₹8,000  
C) ₹10,000  
D) ₹2,000

Rohan pays ₹2,000 per year for a mobile insurance plan that covers accidental damage. If his phone screen repair costs ₹8,000 and he makes one claim in a year, what is his net financial benefit from having insurance?
A) ₹6,000  
B) ₹8,000  
C) ₹10,000  
D) ₹2,000
questions.a:
A) ₹6,000  
Step 1: Identify the cost of insurance (premium) = ₹2,000/year  
Step 2: Identify the loss covered = ₹8,000 (screen repair)  
Step 3: Calculate benefit from claim = Amount covered – Premium paid = ₹8,000 – ₹2,000 = ₹6,000  
Step 4: Interpret: He spent ₹2,000 to avoid paying ₹8,000 out of pocket, so net gain is ₹6,000  
A student who answers ₹8,000 (B) forgot to subtract the premium, showing they don’t see insurance as a net cost-benefit tool. One who answers ₹10,000 (C) added instead of subtracted, indicating a lack of operational clarity in applying the concept.

questions.q:
Priya invests ₹5,000 in a fixed deposit at 6% annual simple interest. After 2 years, she wants to use the money to buy a laptop. How much will she have, and how does this differ from if she had kept the money in a savings locker at home?
A) ₹5,600; it is the same as keeping it at home  
B) ₹5,600; she earned ₹600 extra due to interest  
C) ₹6,000; she doubled her money  
D) ₹10,000; she earned ₹5,000 in profit

Priya invests ₹5,000 in a fixed deposit at 6% annual simple interest. After 2 years, she wants to use the money to buy a laptop. How much will she have, and how does this differ from if she had kept the money in a savings locker at home?
A) ₹5,600; it is the same as keeping it at home  
B) ₹5,600; she earned ₹600 extra due to interest  
C) ₹6,000; she doubled her money  
D) ₹10,000; she earned ₹5,000 in profit
questions.a:
B) ₹5,600; she earned ₹600 extra due to interest  
Step 1: Principal = ₹5,000, Rate = 6%, Time = 2 years  
Step 2: Simple Interest = (P × R × T)/100 = (5000 × 6 × 2)/100 = ₹600  
Step 3: Total Amount = Principal + Interest = ₹5,000 + ₹600 = ₹5,600  
Step 4: At home, she would have only ₹5,000 (no growth), so the difference is ₹600 earned  
A student choosing C or D misunderstands how interest works—either thinking it doubles money or confuses simple with compound interest. This reveals weak grasp of interest calculation from prior nodes (c9_eco_ch4_3), affecting investment understanding.

questions.q:
A student argues: "Buying gold jewelry is better than taking a health insurance policy because gold always increases in value, while insurance gives nothing back if you don’t get sick." Evaluate this statement. Is it financially sound? Why or why not?
A) Yes, because gold is a safe investment and insurance is a waste  
B) No, because gold and insurance serve different purposes—one grows wealth, the other manages risk  
C) Yes, because insurance companies often deny claims  
D) No, because gold loses value over time

A student argues: "Buying gold jewelry is better than taking a health insurance policy because gold always increases in value, while insurance gives nothing back if you don’t get sick." Evaluate this statement. Is it financially sound? Why or why not?
A) Yes, because gold is a safe investment and insurance is a waste  
B) No, because gold and insurance serve different purposes—one grows wealth, the other manages risk  
C) Yes, because insurance companies often deny claims  
D) No, because gold loses value over time
questions.a:
B) No, because gold and insurance serve different purposes—one grows wealth, the other manages risk  
Justification: Gold can fluctuate in price and does not guarantee returns; insurance is not about returns but about transferring risk of high medical costs. Comparing them as alternatives ignores their distinct roles in financial planning.  
A student who chooses A or C fails to see that insurance is not an investment substitute—it addresses a different need (protection vs. growth). This reveals a critical misconception that all financial decisions should be judged by return alone, ignoring risk protection.
